--- title: "PowSyBl & Dynawo" subtitle: "Part 1 · What they are and why GridFM uses them" description: "Two open-source simulators built for transmission system operators, and the role each one plays in GridFM-Datakit." jupyter: python3 --- ::: {.session-strip} [15 min]{.chip} [Part 1 of 4]{.chip} [pypowsybl · pypowsybl.dynamic]{.chip} ::: ::: {.goals} #### In this part - Place PowSyBl and Dynawo in the GridFM-Datakit pipeline. - Load a grid, solve a power flow and draw it with pypowsybl. - Run a first Dynawo time-domain simulation from Python and plot it. ::: ## Two tools from the control room Both projects started at RTE, the French transmission system operator, and are developed in the open. Operators use them for real operational and planning studies, which is what makes them interesting as a source of training data. | | **PowSyBl** | **Dynawo** | |---|---|---| | What | Framework to model, exchange and simulate grids | Time-domain simulator, RMS (phasor) | | Core | Java, with the Python binding **pypowsybl** | C++ solver, Modelica models compiled ahead of time | | Grid formats | CGMES, UCTE, PSS/E, XIIDM, MATPOWER | Reads the grid from PowSyBl | | Simulations | Load flow (OpenLoadFlow), security analysis, sensitivities, short circuit | Short-term stability (DynaSwing), long-term voltage stability (DynaWaltz), steady state with automata (DynaFlow) | | Home | [powsybl.org](https://www.powsybl.org), an LF Energy project | [dynawo.github.io](https://dynawo.github.io) | ![](assets/logos/powsybl-logo.svg){width=180}     ![](assets/logos/dynawo-logo.png){width=150}     ![](assets/logos/lf-energy-logo.svg){width=150} ## Why GridFM-Datakit integrates them A foundation model learns what its data shows it. Datakit already produced large steady-state datasets from MATPOWER cases with PowerModels.jl. PowSyBl and Dynawo extend it in three directions. 1. **Industrial grids in.** PowSyBl reads the formats operators exchange every day, so a dataset can start from a realistic network instead of a textbook case. 2. **Industrial-grade physics out.** OpenLoadFlow and Dynawo are the solvers used on real operational studies, which narrows the gap between synthetic data and the field. 3. **Time as a new modality.** Dynawo turns each operating point into a trajectory, and randomized disturbances become a new axis of data augmentation. ![The datakit pipeline. PowSyBl reads the grid and solves the power flow, Dynawo simulates the time domain.](assets/pipeline.svg){fig-alt="Pipeline from grid model through PowSyBl, datakit perturbation, OPF, power flow, to a steady-state dataset and through Dynawo to trajectories."} ::: {.callout-note title="The same identifiers everywhere"} Every element keeps the ID it has in the network file, from the PowSyBl network to the Dynawo model mapping and the output tables. That is what lets a configuration file say "disconnect `_GEN____2_SM` at 1 s". ::: ## PowSyBl in a few lines The IEEE 14-bus case used throughout the dynamic parts ships as an XIIDM file, the native PowSyBl format. ::: {#5f149b93 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd import pypowsybl as pp network = pp.network.load("../data/ieee14/IEEE14.iidm") network.get_generators()[["name", "target_p", "target_v", "max_p", "voltage_regulator_on"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
name target_p target_v max_p voltage_regulator_on
id
_GEN____1_SM GEN    1 232.3463 73.140 9999.0 True
_GEN____2_SM GEN    2 40.0000 72.105 9999.0 True

_GEN____6_SM GEN    6 0.0000 14.766 9999.0 True

``` ::: ::: Every element type is a pandas DataFrame, and every attribute can be updated in place. A load flow with OpenLoadFlow fills in the voltages and the flows. ::: {#1eeda07f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} result = pp.loadflow.run_ac(network) print(result[0].status_text, "in", result[0].iteration_count, "iterations") network.get_buses()[["v_mag", "v_angle"]].round(2).T ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Converged in 3 iterations ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: PowSyBl also draws the grid. The network area diagram shows each voltage level with its flows. ::: {#df75d26f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} network.get_network_area_diagram() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ![](01-powsybl-dynawo_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ## A first Dynawo simulation `pypowsybl.dynamic` drives Dynawo with three mappings. **Models** attach a dynamic model to a static element, **events** say what happens and when, and **output variables** say what to record. The physical parameters of each model come from a `.par` file, referenced by a parameter set ID. ::: {#83485c59 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pypowsybl.dynamic as dyn models_table = pd.read_csv("../data/ieee14/static_element_dynamic_models.csv") machines = models_table.query("category_name == 'SynchronousGenerator'") machines ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
category_name static_id parameter_set_id model_name
0 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____1_SM Generator1 GeneratorSynchronousFourWindingsProportionalRe...
1 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____2_SM Generator2 GeneratorSynchronousFourWindingsProportionalRe...
2 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____3_SM Generator3 GeneratorSynchronousFourWindingsProportionalRe...
3 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____6_SM Generator6 GeneratorSynchronousThreeWindingsProportionalR...
4 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____8_SM Generator8 GeneratorSynchronousThreeWindingsProportionalR...
``` ::: ::: The five machines get a synchronous generator model. Loads and other elements keep Dynawo's default model. ::: {#7d28b08c .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} models = dyn.ModelMapping() for row in machines.itertuples(): models.add_synchronous_generator( static_id=row.static_id, parameter_set_id=row.parameter_set_id, model_name=row.model_name, ) ``` ::: The disturbance is a 100 ms solid fault on bus 4, cleared without tripping anything. ::: {#9e5a992e .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} events = dyn.EventMapping() events.add_node_fault( static_id="_BUS____4_TN", start_time=1.0, fault_time=0.1, r_pu=0.0, x_pu=0.01 ) outputs = dyn.OutputVariableMapping() outputs.add_standard_model_curves(static_id="_BUS____4_TN", variables=["U_value"]) for gen in machines.static_id: outputs.add_dynamic_model_curves( dynamic_model_id=gen, variables=["generator_omegaPu_value"] ) ``` ::: The solver settings live in the same `.par` file. `IDAOrder2` is a variable-step solver, fine enough to follow a fault. ::: {#e5385400 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} par = "../data/ieee14/IEEE14.par" parameters = dyn.Parameters( start_time=0.0, stop_time=10.0, provider_parameters={ "parametersFile": par, "network.parametersFile": par, "network.parametersId": "Network", "solver.type": "IDA", "solver.parametersFile": par, "solver.parametersId": "IDAOrder2", }, ) simulation = dyn.Simulation() result = simulation.run(network, models, events, outputs, parameters) print(result.status()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DynamicSimulationStatus.SUCCESS ``` ::: ::: The curves come back as one DataFrame indexed by time. ::: {#98b761a1 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} curves = result.curves() curves.index = (curves.index - curves.index[0]).total_seconds() fig, (ax_u, ax_w) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4)) ax_u.plot(curves.index, curves["NETWORK__BUS____4_TN_U_value"], color=PALETTE[0]) ax_u.set(title="Voltage at bus 4", xlabel="time (s)", ylabel="kV") for i, gen in enumerate(machines.static_id): ax_w.plot( curves.index, curves[f"{gen}_generator_omegaPu_value"], color=PALETTE[i], label=gen.strip("_").replace("____", " ").replace("_SM", ""), ) ax_w.set(title="Rotor speed", xlabel="time (s)", ylabel="pu") ax_w.legend(ncols=2) fig.tight_layout() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](01-powsybl-dynawo_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=1199 height=429} ::: ::: The fault collapses the voltage at bus 4, the machines accelerate during the fault, then swing back together. This is one trajectory. Parts 3 and 4 produce thousands of them, each from a different operating point and a different disturbance. ## Your turn ::: {.callout-tip .exercise title="Exercise · Trip a generator"} Replace the fault by the disconnection of generator 2 at 1 s with `events.add_disconnection(static_id=..., start_time=...)`. Run the simulation for 30 s and plot the rotor speed of generator 1. How does the response differ from the fault? ::: ::: {#ac20c2a1 .cell tags='["solution"]' execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show a solution"} network = pp.network.load("../data/ieee14/IEEE14.iidm") pp.loadflow.run_ac(network) trip = dyn.EventMapping() trip.add_disconnection(static_id="_GEN____2_SM", start_time=1.0) parameters = dyn.Parameters( start_time=0.0, stop_time=30.0, provider_parameters=parameters.provider_parameters, ) result = simulation.run(network, models, trip, outputs, parameters) curves = result.curves() curves.index = (curves.index - curves.index[0]).total_seconds() ax = curves["_GEN____1_SM_generator_omegaPu_value"].plot(color=PALETTE[0]) ax.set(title="Rotor speed of generator 1 after tripping generator 2", xlabel="time (s)", ylabel="pu"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](01-powsybl-dynawo_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=870 height=429} ::: ::: Losing a machine is a lasting power imbalance. The speed drops and settles at a new value set by the governors, where a cleared fault leaves the system where it started. ::: {.callout-note title="Next"} [Part 2](02-steady-state.qmd) feeds a real grid through PowSyBl into datakit and builds a steady-state dataset. :::
